lines.text: A Japanese saw cuts as you pull it toward you. That one fact shapes much of the tool.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: This time: the saws, and exactly where the cut goes in relation to the line.

lines.text: Most Western saws cut on the push stroke. Japanese saws cut on the pull. Pulling puts the blade in tension, so it can be made thinner. A pushed blade generally needs to be stiffer, so that it doesn't buckle.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Every saw cut has a width, called the kerf. A thinner blade usually makes a narrower kerf, so there is less wood to remove.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: A common carpenter's saw is the ryōba, which means double-edged. One edge rips, cutting along the grain; that's tatebiki. The other crosscuts, cutting across it; that's yokobiki. The design is fairly modern: it dates from the Meiji era, in the late eighteen hundreds.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: A common carpenter's saw is the ryoh-bah, which means double-edged. One edge rips, cutting along the grain; that's tah-teh-bee-kee. The other crosscuts, cutting across it; that's yoh-koh-bee-kee. The design is fairly modern: it dates from the May-jee era, in the late eighteen hundreds.

lines.text: Look closely at the teeth. Rip teeth work like a row of tiny chisels, paring along the fibers. Crosscut teeth are pointed like small knives, and sever the fibers one by one.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: For fine joinery there is the dōzuki. Its blade is very thin, so a metal spine along the back keeps it stiff. It is classed as a crosscut saw.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: For fine joinery there is the doh-zoo-kee. Its blade is very thin, so a metal spine along the back keeps it stiff. It is classed as a crosscut saw.

lines.text: Dōzuki is also the word for a tenon's shoulder, the face around its base. Cutting it is a clean crosscut: exactly the kind of work this saw does.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: Doh-zoo-kee is also the word for a tenon's shoulder, the face around its base. Cutting it is a clean crosscut: exactly the kind of work this saw does.

lines.text: There is also the kataba, a saw with a single edge and no spine.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: There is also the kah-tah-bah, a saw with a single edge and no spine.

lines.text: Look at the kerf end-on. The teeth are bent out alternately, left and right. This is called the set, or asari. So the kerf is a little wider than the blade, and that width is why the next question matters.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: Look at the kerf end-on. The teeth are bent out alternately, left and right. This is called the set, or ah-sah-ree. So the kerf is a little wider than the blade, and that width is why the next question matters.

lines.text: Where does the kerf go, relative to the line? The carpenter chooses, and the skills test manual sets out three options. In English shop talk: you can take the line, cutting it away; leave the line, sawing just on the waste side; or split it, so half the line remains.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: The choice depends on how tight each joint should be. Some fits should be snug, and some a little looser.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: The national skills test manual for carpenters gives an example. On one tenon, the thickness cuts split the line, so it fits a little looser. The width cuts leave the line, with the saw just on the waste side, so it fits tight.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Either way, the line is the reference. That's why the marking out had to be exact.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: If you own Western saws, the same ideas carry over: rip and crosscut teeth, a backed saw for joinery. The big difference is the stroke.

lines.text: Pull to cut. Rip along the grain, crosscut across it. And before every cut, decide: take the line, leave it, or split it.

lines.text: One note: sharp-tool technique, and how to use these tools safely, is best learned from a teacher, at a bench, in person.
